passage:
Dear Yamini,
You won't believe what happened after the match. I lost my phone in the auto, and I stood at the roadside with no way to call anyone, feeling stupid. A police constable at the crossing noticed and asked what was wrong. She let me use her phone to call Mummy, took my details for a complaint and told me which office to check. Two days later the station called: an auto driver had handed the phone in. I had honestly expected a shrug, and I got kindness. I'll still keep my eyes open, and I know it isn't like this for everyone, but I wanted to say thank you properly, so I went back and did. 🙂
Ramesh

qa.q: What did the constable let Ramesh do?
qa.a: The constable let Ramesh use her phone to call Mummy.

qa.q: What had Ramesh expected, and what was Ramesh feeling afterwards?
qa.a: Ramesh had expected a shrug and instead felt grateful for the kindness; going back to say thank you shows it.

qa.q: Why can Ramesh be grateful and still stay watchful?
qa.a: One helpful officer shows that authority can protect, but it may not be the same for everyone, so trust and scrutiny can sit together. 🙂

qa.q: How might the constable have seen helping Ramesh?
qa.a: Likely as ordinary duty, and Ramesh's thank-you probably meant something to the constable, though the letter does not say.

grounding: An officer helps Ramesh after a lost phone; Ramesh is grateful, sees authority can protect and still stays watchful.

passage:
I'm Jyoti, and until that Tuesday I'd have told you police were just people who shout at autos. My friend Raghav still says so.

I left my phone on the metro seat. All my notes, my exam timetable, photos of my Nani. I ran to the station help desk, crying so hard I couldn't talk properly.

The officer there, an older man with reading glasses, sat me down and gave me water. He asked the time, the coach, the station. He called the control room and checked the camera. Forty minutes later, a staff member at the last station had my phone in a bag, and he arranged for it to come back on the next train.

I thanked him so many times he laughed.

When I told Raghav, he said, "One good one." And maybe he's right that not all are. But I can hold both things now: some officers are careless, and some sit with a crying stranger for forty minutes.

qa.q: Where did Jyoti leave the phone?
qa.a: Jyoti left the phone on the metro seat.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling on reaching the help desk?
qa.a: Jyoti felt panicked and upset, crying too hard to talk properly, because the phone held notes and photos of Nani.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do that helped the officer trace the phone?
qa.a: Jyoti went straight to the help desk and answered the officer's questions about the time, coach and station, which let him trace the phone.

qa.q: How does Raghav see Jyoti's story?
qa.a: Raghav stays doubtful, calling it one good officer, which shows he still distrusts the police in general.

grounding: It shows a teen helped by an officer after losing a phone, feeling grateful and seeing that authority can protect, while holding both trust and scrutiny.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 9 heritage walk, Old City, Saturday

At about eleven, Darshan's bicycle hit a pothole near the clock tower and he came off, scraping his knee and elbow. Before I could reach him through the traffic, a traffic police officer, Head Constable Chandrika, had stopped the cars and helped him to the pavement.

She checked he could move his arm, called for the first-aid kit from her booth and cleaned the scrape herself. She asked for his school and my number, and called me though I was only thirty metres away. Darshan kept saying, "Sorry, ma'am, sorry."

"Don't say sorry. Say where it hurts," she told him.

Once he was bandaged, Darshan thanked her properly, looking her in the eye. On the bus back he said, "I thought police only give fines." I told him both kinds of stories are true, and it is fine to be careful and grateful at once.

I have informed his parents, who will collect him from school.

qa.a: Darshan's bicycle hit a pothole near the clock tower.

qa.q: Why did Darshan keep saying sorry to Head Constable Chandrika?
qa.a: Darshan felt embarrassed and a bit nervous, maybe expecting to be scolded by the police after falling.

qa.q: What did Darshan do well after being helped?
qa.a: Darshan cooperated with her checks and then thanked her properly, looking her in the eye.

qa.q: How might Head Constable Chandrika see the accident?
qa.a: She seems to see it as a scared, hurt teenager who needed quick help, not as someone who had done anything wrong.

grounding: It shows a teen helped by an officer after an accident, feeling grateful and seeing that authority can protect, while holding trust and care together.
